deep.reconstruction:
This is the opening page of Euler's unfinished 'Tractatus de numerorum doctrina' (E792; usually dated c. 1749-1750 and first printed in the 1849 Opera postuma). Chapter I, 'On the composition of numbers', lays down the elementary foundations of the positive integers. There are no derivations, only definitions and immediate consequences.

§1-2: A number is a multitude of units, so every number n tells how many units it contains.

§3: Starting from 1, the integers are 1, 2, 3, ..., each exceeding its predecessor by one unit (n+1 = S(n)).

§4: Since any number can be increased by a unit, the sequence is infinite (no largest number).

§5: Since 1 must also exceed its predecessor by one unit, that predecessor is 0. So 0 is introduced as the predecessor of 1.

§6: Only integers are treated. Fractions, and still more surds (irrationals), are excluded.

§7: The successors of a are a+1, a+2, a+3, ..., exceeding a by 1, 2, 3, ... units.

§8: The predecessors of a are a-1, a-2, ..., falling short of a by 1, 2, ... units. (Implicit, mine: this holds only while k ≤ a.)

§9: Addition and subtraction are defined as iterated adjunction or removal of units. a+b means adding b units to a; a-b means removing b units from a.

§10-11: Repeated addition of a to itself gives the multiples a+a = 2a, 3a, 4a, .... Each multiple exceeds the previous one by a. Relative to them, a is the 'simplum'. In modern terms, k·a is defined recursively by 1·a = a and (k+1)a = ka + a.

§12: If a = 1, its multiples give every number. If a is a genuine multitude of units (a ≥ 2), some numbers are not multiples of a. No proof is given here; it follows on the next page (§13: 1, ..., a-1 are non-multiples).

The page serves as the axiomatic-informal groundwork for the later chapters on divisibility, primes and residues.
errors: §8 tacitly assumes a-k is defined only for k ≤ a (or k < a if 0 is to be avoided). Subtraction a-b in §9 likewise requires b ≤ a; this is left unstated.

Minor terminological looseness: §11 lists the multiples as 2a, 3a, ..., separating the simplum a. Yet §12's claim that the multiples of 1 give 'all numbers' requires counting the simplum 1 itself. Euler later makes this explicit ('ejus simplo non excluso', §17; §26).
§12's existence claim for non-multiples is stated without proof on this page; it is justified on the following page (§13).

results.what: Natural numbers as a multitude of units, generated from 1 by successive addition of a unit; the sequence is infinite; 0 is the predecessor of 1
results.modern_name: Successor-based (pre-axiomatic) construction of the natural numbers
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (Euclid Book VII def. 1-2) for the 'multitude of units' definition; the rigorous successor-based treatment is credited to Grassmann (1861), Dedekind (1888) and Peano (1889)

results.what: Addition and subtraction defined as iterated adding or removing of units; multiples as iterated addition
results.modern_name: Recursive definition of addition and multiplication (informal)

results.what: For a ≥ 2, not every number is a multiple of a
results.modern_name: Existence of non-multiples / nontrivial residues mod a

deep.surprise_reason: These are elementary textbook definitions at the start of Euler's known posthumous number-theory treatise (published 1849). They are Euclidean in spirit and contain nothing non-standard. The motivated introduction of 0 as the predecessor of 1 is a pleasant detail but not historically surprising.

checkable.asserts: Adding a to itself n times gives the multiple n*a (§10-11)
Each multiple exceeds the preceding one by a (§11)

checkable.sympy: all(any(k % a == 0 for k in [m]) or m % a != 0 for a in range(2,20) for m in range(1,a))  and all(m % a != 0 for a in range(2,20) for m in range(1,a))
checkable.asserts: For a ≥ 2, the numbers 1..a-1 are not multiples of a, so non-multiples exist (§12)
Every number is a multiple of 1 (§12, case a = 1)

transcription_corrections: The transcription is essentially accurate. The original prints the plus sign in the old typographic form '-+-' (e.g. 'a -+- 1'); it is rendered correctly as '+'.
The faint mirrored text in the upper part of the image is bleed-through from the verso (page 4, §13-18) and is not part of this page's content.
The asterisk at the bottom right is a printer's signature mark, not part of Euler's text.
